name: Chin tucks

card.summary: A neck-retraction movement used for posture and deep neck flexor work; most published research concerns swallowing therapy, not jawline appearance.
card.aka: Neck retraction, McKenzie chin tuck, chin retraction
card.note: Research on chin tucks is mainly from swallowing studies; some forum users warn about prolonged holds.

quick.overview:
A chin tuck is a movement in which the head is drawn straight back so the chin moves toward the neck without tilting the head down. It is used in posture routines and aimed at the deep neck flexor muscles, and it is often paired in forums with rows and face pulls for forward head posture.

Published studies of chin tucks are mostly in swallowing (dysphagia) research, where the posture is used as a compensatory maneuver. Studies of its effect on facial appearance were not found.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the movement strengthens the deep neck flexors and counteracts a head carried forward of the shoulders, which they link to a more defined jaw-neck profile. Swallowing studies show that the chin-tuck posture changes pharyngeal dimensions and pressure events.
quick.risks: No serious harms are documented in the sources reviewed. One looksmax.org thread author claims that holding a chin tuck for long periods could strain the cervical spine, a claim that other users in the thread called fear mongering; no study cited here tests it.

lead: A chin tuck is a posture or exercise in which the head is retracted backward over the neck so that the chin draws in. In clinical literature the term most often refers to a swallowing maneuver used with people who have dysphagia, and it has been studied with videofluoroscopy and manometry [1][2][3][4]. A resisted version, chin tuck against resistance (CTAR), was proposed as a way to increase activity of the suprahyoid muscles [5].

In looksmaxxing communities the movement is discussed in connection with posture and head position, in the belief that a head held forward weakens the appearance of the jawline and neck. Forward head posture is described by Wikipedia as a common postural pattern linked to prolonged device use, with deep neck flexor strengthening among the proposed remedies [6]. No clinical study located here has measured whether chin tucks change facial or jaw appearance.
infobox: Deep neck flexors (proposed); suprahyoid muscles in the resisted variant
None (resisted variants use a ball or band)

paras: The movement involves retracting the head horizontally while keeping the gaze level, rather than nodding the head downward. A looksmax.org user attributes a version called the McKenzie chin tuck to the orthotropics advocate Mike Mew and says it rotates the head into flexion [7].

Most studies examine chin tuck as a swallowing posture. A manometry study of seven subjects compared neutral, head-turn and chin-tuck conditions for pharyngeal pressure events [1]. Videomanometry studies tested supraglottic swallow, effortful swallow and chin tuck in eight healthy volunteers and in eight patients with pharyngeal dysfunction [2][3]. A 2002 report from the same line of work examined hypopharyngeal intrabolus pressure [8]. A radiographic study of 30 subjects measured pharyngeal dimensions in neutral and chin-tucked positions [9], and a clinical and electrophysiologic study examined how head and neck positions affect oropharyngeal swallowing [10].

The resisted variant, CTAR, was described in a 2014 paper as a Shaker-type exercise designed to raise suprahyoid muscle activity [5]. Reviews of dysphagia management after stroke and swallowing rehabilitation after oropharyngeal cancer surgery mention chin-tuck-based approaches in rehabilitation contexts [11][12]. These studies concern swallowing, not posture or facial appearance.

Wikipedia describes forward head posture as common among device users and some occupations, with proposed effects including neck muscle fatigue and cervicogenic headache and proposed remedies including deep neck flexor strengthening, mid-back strengthening, thoracic mobilization and ergonomic changes. The article carries maintenance notes about weak sourcing for some treatment claims [6].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the chin tuck appears in threads about neck posture and jaw appearance, where users ask what it does and debate its safety [7][13].

claims.claim: Chin tucks improve head posture by stretching the neck.
claims.believers: A forum reply to a question about the purpose of chin tucks says the movement stretches the neck and leads to better head posture [13].
claims.experts: Published chin-tuck research concerns swallowing, and no study cited here tests posture or appearance outcomes [1][2][5].

claims.claim: Prolonged chin-tuck holds can damage the neck.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster says the movement as promoted can cause hyperflexion of the neck and, if held for long periods, harm discs, spinal cord and occipital muscles; replies in the thread call this fear mongering and say chin tucks combined with face pulls strengthen the occipital area [7].
claims.experts: No study cited here has examined harms from sustained chin tucks.

claims.claim: Sleeping or holding a different head position could improve the jaw.
claims.believers: A thread starter asks whether sleeping position or chin tucks could help the jaw, reflecting a belief that head position shapes jaw appearance [13].
claims.experts: No published study located here links chin tucks or head posture to jaw structure.
